videos.name: Managing Users and Groups in Linux
videos.description: 18 min · creating, changing and deleting local user accounts — the defaults useradd applies and the file that sets them, giving an account a password, choosing its numeric ID, moving and renaming its home directory, and making a password expire every 30 days or never — then groups: the primary group made with each account against secondary ones such as wheel or docker, adding and removing members, changing a user's primary group, and creating and deleting groups. From 2024

videos.name: Linux File Permissions in 5 Minutes
videos.description: 6 min · reading the permission string from ls -l — owner, group and everyone else, r, w and x, and what each means for a directory — then chown to change the owner and group, chmod with the 4-2-1 numbers (644, 774), and common settings such as 400 for an SSH key pair. From 2023

videos.name: How sudo Actually Works (It's Not What You Think)
videos.description: 4 min · what sudo really does — it asks for your own password, not root's (root needn't even have one), checks the sudoers rules (user, hosts, target user and group, commands; % marks a group, NOPASSWD skips the prompt), authenticates you through PAM, then switches the effective user ID to run the command; why to edit sudoers only with visudo, and the timestamp that skips the prompt for 15 minutes. From 2026

videos.name: Do You Really Know Linux File Permissions? (rwx, 755, umask, setuid, sticky bit)
videos.description: 12 min · all twelve permission bits — reading ls -l, rwx as the numbers 4, 2 and 1, chmod with letters, the order in which the kernel checks owner, group and others, what r, w and x mean on a directory, how umask really sets the defaults (it switches bits off rather than subtracting, so 033 gives 644), and the special bits: setuid, which is how passwd can write /etc/shadow, setgid, and the sticky bit on /tmp. Every command shown comes from a real terminal session. From 2026

videos.name: Access Permission (Linux: SetUID, SetGID, Sticky Bit)
videos.description: 6 min · a lesson from Google's IT Support course on Coursera, re-uploaded by this channel, on the three special permission bits — setuid, the s in place of x that lets passwd write /etc/shadow as root, set with u+s or a leading 4; setgid, which runs a program with its group's permissions (a leading 2); and the sticky bit on /tmp, where anyone can add files but only the owner or root can delete them (+t or a leading 1). From 2022

videos.name: SELinux vs AppArmor
videos.description: 4 min · the two mandatory access control systems side by side — ordinary Linux permissions let a file's owner decide, while mandatory access control enforces rules even root-run processes must obey; SELinux labels every file, process and port with a security context and allows only what its policy lists (the default on Red Hat and Fedora, debugged through the audit log with audit2why), while AppArmor gives each program a profile of the paths it may touch (the default on Ubuntu, Debian and SUSE), simpler to write but blind to a moved or renamed file. Both have a learning mode, and the advice is to learn whichever your distribution ships. From 2026

videos.name: Linux Passwd & Shadow File Explained
videos.description: 4 min · the two files behind user accounts and password expiry, opened side by side — /etc/passwd's username, the x where the password used to be, user and group IDs, comment, home directory and login shell, then /etc/shadow's hash, with $6$ marking SHA-512, and the ageing fields after it — and why passwd is readable by everyone while shadow is kept from ordinary users, since a weak hash can be cracked. He calls two of the ageing fields the minimum and maximum characters allowed; they are the minimum and maximum days between password changes. From 2018

videos.name: Every Linux file system
videos.description: 3 min · the Linux filesystems side by side, in three minutes

videos.name: Linux PIPES and REDIRECTS
videos.description: 17 min · STDIN, STDOUT and STDERR: saving a command's output to a file, hiding or logging its errors, and chaining commands together with pipes and redirects. From 2022

videos.name: VFS: How Linux Talks to Every Filesystem
videos.description: 3 min · the virtual filesystem layer that lets the same cat work on ext4, XFS, Btrfs, NFS or /proc — a common set of operations every filesystem implements, the superblock, inode, dentry and file objects, and how open walks a path through the dentry cache to the right filesystem driver. From 2026

videos.name: The Kernel's Filing Cabinet: Linux VFS Explained
videos.description: 6 min · how the Virtual File System gives USB sticks, network drives and disks one interface, and why "everything is a file". From 2026

videos.name: How Journaling Saves Your Filesystem From a Crash
videos.description: 3 min · why a crash between writing a file's data and updating its metadata used to corrupt a filesystem, and how a journal fixes it — log the change, make it, then clear the entry, so recovery after a power cut replays the journal in seconds instead of a long fsck. ext4 and XFS work this way; the video lists Btrfs too, though Btrfs gets the same safety from copy-on-write rather than a journal. From 2026

videos.name: Hard Links vs Symlinks
videos.description: 3 min · two ways to give a file another name — a hard link is a second name for the same inode, so the data lives until the last name is deleted, but it can't cross filesystems or point at a directory; a symlink is a small file holding a path, which can do both but breaks if its target moves. From 2026

videos.name: Pipes: The Plumbing That Built Unix
videos.description: 3 min · the pipe's history (Doug McIlroy's request, built by Ken Thompson in an evening in 1973) and how it works — standard input, output and error, the kernel's 64 KB pipe buffer that makes a fast writer wait for a slow reader, chained pipelines, and the do-one-thing-well idea behind them. From 2026

videos.name: Fun Experiment With CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE Capability
videos.description: 2 min · a directory you own whose file names you can list but can't enter or read — what the permission bits are doing there, and how a process holding CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE skips those checks entirely. From 2026

videos.name: SetPriv: The Linux Command Most People Don't Know
videos.description: 4 min · giving a program one capability without making it root — a Python server that needs port 112, why setcap cap_net_bind_service on the system-wide python3 is risky (any script could then run a fake SSH server), why putting it on the script itself fails (the kernel checks the interpreter), and setpriv, which starts the process as an ordinary user while passing that one capability on as an ambient capability, with nothing changed on disk. From 2026

videos.name: I Blocked Dangerous Linux Syscalls with Seccomp
videos.description: 7 min · seccomp, the kernel filter that decides which system calls a process may make — strace to see the syscalls a command uses, firejail's --seccomp.drop to block execve (and why a shell built-in like pwd still runs) or unlinkat so that even a file you own can't be deleted, returning a chosen error such as ENOENT instead, then a small C wrapper using libseccomp that blocks clone with CLONE_VM, sets no_new_privs and starts bash, which stops the Copy Fail root exploit. From 2026

videos.name: From GRUB to Login: How Linux Actually Boots
videos.description: 4 min · the hand-offs from power button to login — firmware (BIOS or UEFI) and its power-on self test, GRUB loading the compressed kernel and the initramfs that holds the drivers needed to mount the real root, the kernel probing hardware and mounting root, then starting systemd as the first process. From 2026

videos.name: How Linux Multitasks: The Evolution of CPU Scheduling
videos.description: 9 min · how the CPU scheduler runs many tasks on few cores, from context switching to CFS and its replacement, EEVDF. From 2026

videos.name: The Illusion of Memory: Linux Kernel Memory Management Explained
videos.description: 9 min · virtual memory and how the kernel shares and optimises memory: de-duplication with KSM, NUMA and GPUs, and DAMON for monitoring access patterns. From 2026

videos.name: Copy-on-Write (CoW) Deep Dive: Page Faults, Forks, and Memory Optimization
videos.description: 6 min · why copying a file or starting a VM is near-instant: copy-on-write, page faults used as a trigger, and forks. From 2026

videos.name: mmap: How a File Becomes Memory
videos.description: 4 min · mapping a file into memory instead of reading it into a buffer — skipping the extra copy out of the page cache, page faults loading 4 KB pages only when they're touched (demand paging), so a 10 GB file costs only the pages you actually read. From 2026

videos.name: How Swap Works (and Why It Kills Performance)
videos.description: 3 min · swap as disk-backed overflow for RAM — inactive pages written out to a swap partition or file, why reading them back is about a thousand times slower even from an SSD, and what helps: more RAM, watching memory in top or htop, lowering swappiness, or compressed swap with zram. From 2026

videos.name: The OOM Killer: How Linux Decides What Dies
videos.description: 5 min · what happens when RAM and swap run out — memory overcommit promising more than exists, reclaim and swap tried first, then the OOM killer scoring every process by memory use (/proc/<pid>/oom_score, adjustable through oom_score_adj) and killing the highest with SIGKILL so the rest keep running. From 2026

videos.name: eBPF Explained: How to Safely Program the Linux Kernel
videos.description: 8 min · reprogramming the kernel without recompiling or loading risky modules, from the original Berkeley Packet Filter to eBPF, and how the verifier keeps it safe. From 2026

videos.name: eBPF: The Linux Kernel Superpower You Need to Know
videos.description: 9 min · running sandboxed programs inside the kernel on events, for observability and XDP networking, and why the verifier makes it safe. From 2026

videos.name: Rust in the Linux Kernel: Why After 30 Years of C?
videos.description: 7 min · why the kernel added Rust as a second language in 6.1, how unsafe C bridges to safe Rust, and the steps to build a kernel with Rust support. From 2026

videos.name: KVM vs QEMU
videos.description: 2 min · the two halves of a Linux virtual machine — KVM, a kernel module that runs guests at near-native speed using Intel VT-x or AMD-V, and QEMU, which emulates the devices (and whole other CPU architectures when needed), working together under tools like virt-manager. From 2026

videos.name: KVM Explained: How Linux Becomes a Hypervisor
videos.description: 7 min · how the kernel itself becomes a bare-metal hypervisor through KVM, how KVM pairs with QEMU, and nested virtualization. From 2026

videos.name: Monitoring vs Observability — Why Knowing Something Is Broken Isn’t Enough
videos.description: 5 min · the difference between monitoring, which tells you something is broken, and observability, which lets you find out why. From 2025

videos.name: Why Observability Needed OpenTelemetry — The Missing Puzzle Piece
videos.description: 11 min · why monitoring was fragmented before OpenTelemetry: every vendor had its own agents and formats, and how a common standard fixes that. From 2025

videos.name: 🔥 Linux Performance Troubleshooting — Episode 1: The I/O Wait Nightmare
videos.description: 18 min · a slow machine with a low CPU: why I/O wait is the bottleneck to look at, and how to find which disk and process causes it. From 2025

videos.name: systemd vs OpenRC vs SysVinit
videos.description: 4 min · the three init systems you'll meet — SysVinit's ordered shell scripts (still in Slackware), OpenRC from Gentoo adding dependencies and parallel starts on top of a simple PID 1 (Alpine, Gentoo, Artix), and systemd's declarative unit files used by most distributions — and why the choice still causes arguments. From 2026

videos.name: systemd: How Linux Starts 100 Things at Once
videos.description: 3 min · how systemd starts over a hundred services in seconds — replacing SysVinit's one-after-another shell scripts with unit files (service, socket, mount, timer) that declare their dependencies, a dependency graph that starts everything independent at once, and targets such as multi-user and graphical in place of runlevels. From 2026

videos.name: What PID 1 Actually Does
videos.description: 4 min · why the first process is special — the root of the process tree, starting everything at boot, adopting and reaping orphans so they don't linger as zombies, ignoring signals it hasn't chosen to handle so it can't be killed by accident, and starting and stopping services in order; if it dies, the kernel panics. From 2026

videos.name: File Descriptors: The Number Behind Every Open File
videos.description: 3 min · the small integer behind every open file and socket — the per-process descriptor table pointing into the kernel's open file table and on to the inode, 0, 1 and 2 opened before main runs, and leaking descriptors until the per-process limit (often 1024) stops anything new from opening. From 2026

videos.name: The Life and Death of a Linux Process
videos.description: 4 min · a process from creation to clean-up — the task struct the kernel keeps for each one, fork then exec, the running, sleeping, stopped and zombie states, and the exit status the parent collects with wait. From 2026

videos.name: fork(): How One Program Becomes Two
videos.description: 4 min · fork in C — the kernel copying the process's memory and file descriptors, fork returning twice (the child's PID to the parent, 0 to the child, a negative number on failure), and why the two processes' output can come out in either order. From 2026

videos.name: Zombie Processes: The Dead That Won't Leave
videos.description: 2 min · a child that has exited but whose parent hasn't called wait, left behind as an entry in the process table — a Python demo that makes one, why zombies use no CPU or memory but can use up PIDs, and reaping them with wait or a SIGCHLD handler. From 2026

videos.name: Linux Well known signals
videos.description: 9 min · the signals you’ll meet most — SIGINT from Ctrl-C, SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 left for programs to define, SIGKILL from kill -9 (shown ending a process found with ps aux), SIGTERM, which plain kill sends and a program can catch to tidy up first, SIGABRT from abort(), SIGSEGV behind a segmentation fault, and SIGCHLD telling a parent its child has ended so it can wait for it. He says SIGABRT and SIGSEGV can’t be caught; in fact only SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can’t — the rest can have handlers. From 2018

videos.name: SystemD
videos.description: course · 6 lessons · 1h 30m · using systemd to limit what users and services can take — resource limits on users' slices (for all users, each user or one user, freezing a slice, systemctl set-property), services a normal user runs without root (lingering, targets, starting at boot), locking down a service's network (IP accounting, allowing or denying addresses in and out, drop-in files, eBPF filters, restricting which ports it can bind, nftables integration), disk bandwidth and IOPS limits measured with fio and tried as transient units, memory explained (used, available, cache, swap, resident against virtual, overcommit and the OOM killer) before setting MemoryMax and MemoryHigh, and CPU limits on a service and on slices that group services. From 2025

videos.name: SSH for Beginners: Everything You Need to Get Started
videos.description: 88 min · a full beginner's course on OpenSSH — what it is and the path a connection takes across the internet, the client, the ~/.ssh folder and known_hosts (and the warning you get when a server's host key changes, which can mean a man-in-the-middle), a client config file for short host names, then password logins against key pairs: making a key, why a passphrase protects a stolen key, what someone can do with a leaked private key, copying the public key into authorized_keys the manual way and the quick way, a separate key per client, and ssh-agent. Then the server side — the sshd service, its host keys, and turning password authentication off while testing before you log out — and troubleshooting with ssh -v, the log of failed login attempts, and the permissions ~/.ssh must have. From 2020

videos.name: Linux Crash Course - Scheduling Tasks with Cron
videos.description: 19 min · scheduling commands with cron — editing a crontab with crontab -e, the five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and what an asterisk means, always giving the full path to the script, running jobs as root or as a purpose-made user such as www-data with crontab -u, listing a user's jobs with crontab -l, and building the line with crontabgenerator.org. From 2021

videos.name: Automate Your Tasks with systemd Timers: A Step-by-Step Guide
videos.description: 33 min · systemd timers as an alternative to cron. It covers how they differ: they need systemd, can run a job the machine was switched off for, and give finer control. Then it builds an example that sends a weather report to every logged-in user with wall and curl wttr.in. That starts with a service unit in /etc/systemd/system that waits for network-online.target, with its ExecStart wrapped in /bin/sh -c because a service doesn't get a full shell. Next come daemon-reload and a matching .timer unit with OnCalendar=Mon..Fri 10:00 and WantedBy=timers.target. It explains the difference between enabling a timer, which arms it at boot, and starting it, which starts the countdown now. After that: Persistent=true to catch up on missed runs, and OnBootSec to delay the first run after a boot. It shows the OnCalendar format (day of week, date and time, with * wildcards) through yearly, monthly, daily and every-minute schedules. Last, it combines OnBootSec with OnUnitActiveSec to repeat a job every few minutes. From 2023

videos.name: Zsh Shell Tutorial #24: Automate with cron & launchd
videos.description: 13 min · part 24 of a Zsh shell series, on scheduling jobs. It covers cron syntax and managing a crontab, with a live cron job firing, then common cron patterns and shortcuts. On macOS it moves to launchd, scheduling a job with a plist agent. The link opens at 7:41, where the launchd part begins. The code is at github.com/GoCelesteAI/zsh_scheduling_tasks. From 2026

videos.name: 3 Important Tweaks for Improving OpenSSH Security on Your Cloud Instance
videos.description: 39 min · three changes for a new cloud server, done live — creating your own user with sudo and then stopping root from logging in, switching to key-based logins (making the key, what is in the private and public halves, copying the public one over and testing it against password logins), and moving SSH to another port — plus letting only your own account log in over SSH, checking the logs when a change locks you out, and copying files with scp on the new port. From 2019

videos.name: 5 Must Have Tweaks to Secure OpenSSH
videos.description: 22 min · the baseline — turning the SSH service off if you don't need it, moving it off port 22, stopping root from logging in once you have a sudo user, switching password logins off entirely in sshd_config, a firewall rule so only your addresses can reach it, and a hardware key on top. From 2022

videos.name: This Hidden Linux Feature Controls SSH Access
videos.description: 5 min · an SSH login that fails even though the SSH configuration looks right, traced to PAM — what PAM is, following the failure through it, and the pam_access module, which decides which users may log in and from where. From 2026

videos.name: SSH Hardening Options You've Never Heard Of
videos.description: 6 min · options you can put in front of a key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys to limit what that key may do — forcing it to run one command, refusing it a terminal with no-pty, accepting it only from certain IP addresses, and giving it an expiry time. From 2026

videos.name: Securing your Cloud Server with Fail2ban
videos.description: 41 min · fail2ban, which watches log files and bans addresses that keep failing to log in — installing it on an Ubuntu cloud server, what it is for, configuring it in its own local file rather than the one updates replace, exempting your own address, jails, enabling the SSH jail (also when SSH is on another port) and one for Apache, why not to enable everything, reading its log, and unbanning an address. From 2019

videos.name: Resetting OpenSSH Host Keys (the easy method)
videos.description: 23 min · why every machine cloned from the same image needs its own SSH host keys — the duplicate host keys and machine-id a template passes on, then a systemd unit that clears the host keys so new ones are made on first boot, built into a Proxmox template. From 2021

videos.name: SSH tunneling: local and remote port forwarding (by example)
videos.description: 18 min · local port forwarding: reaching a service a firewall blocks, such as a Postgres database on port 5432, through the SSH port the firewall does allow. SSH carries the traffic inside its own connection and hands it out on a port on your machine, so your client talks to localhost. Then remote port forwarding, which does the reverse and exposes a service on your machine to the far end, and the GatewayPorts setting it needs. From 2020

videos.name: OSI model and related
videos.description: course · 7 lessons · 48 min · the OSI model’s seven layers, encapsulation and the protocol data unit at each layer, TCP against UDP, how TCP opens and closes a session, collision and broadcast domains with hubs, switches and routers, ARP, and the TCP/IP model and its suite of protocols. From 2018–2019

videos.name: IPv4 Basics
videos.description: course · 15 lessons · 2h 14m · IP addressing from the ground up — the five classes of IPv4 addresses, converting between binary, decimal and hexadecimal, what a subnet mask does, how a computer decides whether to talk to a host directly or through a router, counting usable host IDs, subnetting (a class B network and subnetting a subnet included), VLSM worked through as a CompTIA Network+ simulation question, special and private addresses, NAT in its SNAT, DNAT, PAT and port-forwarding forms, and how DHCP hands out addresses. From 2018–2020

videos.name: Networking Security Devices
videos.description: playlist · 5 videos · 25 min · the devices that guard a network — IDS against IPS, honeynets and the DMZ, proxy servers, firewalls, and access control lists on a router. From 2018

videos.name: Docker for Beginners: Learn Containers Step by Step
videos.description: playlist · 6 videos · 1h 06m · Docker from scratch — what containers are and why they’re used, running a first container, storage with volumes and bind mounts, container networking with the bridge, MACVLAN and IPVLAN drivers compared, writing a Dockerfile to build your own image, and Docker Compose with volumes, networks and environment variables. From 2026

videos.name: The Linux Network Stack, Top to Bottom
videos.description: 4 min · a request's path down through the kernel — the socket layer (a socket is just a file descriptor), TCP or UDP breaking data into segments, IP addressing and routing, the device driver and the network card — each layer doing one job. From 2026

videos.name: How a Packet Travels Through iptables
videos.description: 3 min · where a rule actually applies — the raw, mangle, nat and filter tables in their fixed order, a packet entering through PREROUTING, the routing decision sending it to INPUT or FORWARD, locally generated replies leaving through OUTPUT and POSTROUTING, and why the first matching rule wins and the chain's default policy catches the rest. From 2026

videos.name: epoll: How Linux Handles 10,000 Connections
videos.description: 4 min · how one thread can watch 10,000 connections — why a thread per connection wastes memory and select and poll copy and scan every descriptor on each call, and how epoll registers sockets once and wakes the process only with the ones that are ready; the reason Redis, Node.js and Go perform the way they do on Linux. From 2026

videos.name: Nftables Firewall
videos.description: course · 8 lessons · 2h 23m · nftables built up rule by rule — a firewall for incoming traffic tested with netcat (tables and chains, counters, matching connections by state, anonymous and named sets, concatenations), dynamic sets, sets with timeouts and constant sets, jumping between chains and verdict maps, source NAT (why NAT exists, masquerade, regular SNAT, NAT pools, 1:1 NAT, balancing source addresses), destination NAT (redirect, DNAT to localhost, port forwarding to expose services, maps), load balancing with round-robin, weighted, random and hash distribution, Direct Server Return compared with traditional load balancing, and rate limits and meters for ICMP, SYN floods, bandwidth and connection counts. From 2023–2024

videos.name: Docker Networking
videos.description: course · 4 lessons · 1h 10m · how Docker networking works underneath — network namespaces, veth pairs and bridges, how two containers on a bridge reach each other and find each other by name through Docker's DNS, how containers reach the internet through source NAT and connection tracking, publishing a port with destination NAT, and Docker Swarm's overlay network, the containers' way out through the gateway bridge, and the routing mesh that answers on every node. From 2023

videos.name: Kubernetes
videos.description: course · 11 lessons · 4h 2m · Kubernetes on your own hardware, networking first — getting around a cluster with the k9s terminal UI, how pods talk and the service types (headless, ClusterIP, external IP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) with MetalLB handing out addresses, building a dual-stack IPv4 and IPv6 cluster on Ubuntu 24.04 (preparing the OS, the container runtime, bootstrapping from a config file, the Flannel network plugin, adding worker nodes), a fully routed cluster with Calico and BGP (measured against Flannel, ECMP, MetalLB in BGP mode and the external traffic policy), Calico network policies with labels and selectors, then K3s home labs — Traefik ingress reached through a Cloudflare tunnel, MetalLB with MikroTik and ExternalDNS giving local names (Pi-hole, code-server), private access to workloads through Tailscale, three ways to put a highly available K3s cluster on the internet (a floating IP with keepalived, MetalLB, Cloudflare tunnels), and Cloudflare WARP with hostname routes for zero-trust access to private services. From 2024–2025

videos.name: Introduction to Namespace: UTS Namespace Explained
videos.description: 21 min · Part 1 of his namespaces series: how a container gets its own hostname without changing the host, from Linux up to Docker and Kubernetes. From 2025

videos.name: Container Security 101: Linux Namespaces
videos.description: 8 min · how PID namespaces isolate processes, how to identify and enter one, and how a --pid=host setting in a container configuration lets it reach the host. From 2026

videos.name: Linux Network Namespaces with ip netns
videos.description: 9 min · creating and managing network namespaces with ip netns, and the virtual interfaces inside them. From 2020

videos.name: Containers - Namespaces, Cgroups and Overlay Filesystem
videos.description: 5 min · the overview: a container is just a process, isolated by namespaces, limited by cgroups and given its root filesystem by an overlay. From 2022

videos.name: The Invisible Engine of the Cloud: Linux Cgroups Explained
videos.description: 5 min · how cgroups act as a bodyguard for the system, stopping runaway processes from taking every resource. From 2026

videos.name: How Containers work ? Demo with PID Namespaces
videos.description: 11 min · a demo of a PID namespace: a process that sees itself as PID 1 and cannot see anything on the host, while the host still sees it under its real PID. From 2024

videos.name: Network Namespaces - How they work?
videos.description: 12 min · how a network namespace gives a container its own interfaces, routes and firewall, and how it is wired back to the host. From 2024

videos.name: Cgroups Introduction
videos.description: 8 min · what control groups are and the usual workflow: create a group, set a limit, move a process into it. From 2022

videos.name: Overlay Filesystems
videos.description: 13 min · how an overlay, or union, filesystem stacks read-only image layers under one writable layer, which is how a container's root filesystem is built. From 2022

videos.name: The Only Container Networking Tutorial You'll Ever Need
videos.description: 7 min · how Docker container networking works — the veth pair with one end in the container and one on the host, matching a veth to its container, the docker0 bridge carrying traffic between containers, IP forwarding and routing for traffic to other networks, NAT and whether the container's IP survives it, and network isolation. From 2026

videos.name: Why Hackers Love exec
videos.description: 5 min · the shell's exec builtin — replacing the current shell with another program, opening and redirecting file descriptors, sending all of a shell's output somewhere else, and changing the name a process shows in process listings. From 2026

videos.name: # Episode 1: Who Actually Killed Your Pod? (It’s Not Kubernetes)?
videos.description: 45 min · a pod that restarted overnight with exit code 137: Kubernetes does not kill for exceeding memory, so the trace goes down to the Linux kernel OOM killer. From 2026

videos.name: Pod Evicted? OOMKilled vs Evicted — Two Different Killers
videos.description: 38 min · why a Kubernetes pod can be OOMKilled by the kernel or evicted by the kubelet, and how to tell which happened. From 2026

videos.name: Linux Tip - Understanding Chroot - Episode 2
videos.description: 12 min · chroot, the oldest form of isolation and the ancestor of containers: giving a process a different root directory, how that differs from a virtual machine, and how phone operating systems such as Android use it. Recorded on Ubuntu 18.04. From 2020

videos.name: This Tiny Binary Replaces Dozens of Linux Commands
videos.description: 4 min · BusyBox, one small binary that stands in for ls, ps, pwd and dozens of other commands — how it works, its built-in shell, and why it turns up in sandboxes and minimal container images, shown running in both. From 2026

videos.name: How to Safely Run Untrusted Exploits on Linux
videos.description: 3 min · keeping a proof-of-concept exploit cloned from GitHub from harming the machine you test it on — isolating it from your own system, reading it before you run it, and cutting it off from the network so it can't reach anything you didn't intend. From 2026

videos.name: Why Your Container App Is Always PID 1
videos.description: 13 min · Part 2 of his namespaces series: the PID namespace, and why an application becomes PID 1 inside a container and what that means for signals. From 2025

videos.name: 🎬 Episode 0: Containers Start as Linux Processes
videos.description: 7 min · the opening episode of his series on Linux for containers: a container is only a process. From 2025

videos.name: Container Security Fundamentals - Seccomp
videos.description: 7 min · part 10, the last of the series: seccomp choosing which of the 300-plus system calls (they differ between ARM and x86) a container may make — Docker's default profile, which has blocked several kernel CVEs, stopping unshare until the container runs with seccomp=unconfined, Kubernetes switching that default off unless you set it on each workload, and writing a custom profile. From 2023

videos.name: Container Security Fundamentals - AppArmor
videos.description: 4 min · part 9 of Datadog’s container security series: mandatory access control, which still restricts a process running as root — AppArmor on Debian and Ubuntu against SELinux on Red Hat, aa-status listing the installed profiles, Docker putting every container under its docker-default profile (built for compatibility rather than strictness), and a one-rule custom profile that stops root inside a container from writing to /etc. From 2023

videos.name: Container Security Fundamentals - Datadog

From 2023

videos.name: Container Security
videos.description: playlist · 19 videos · 1h 27m · short demos, most under five minutes — containers as ordinary Linux processes, what root cannot do on its own and the capabilities its power is split into, each namespace in turn (PID, user, network, mount, IPC and time), cgroups limiting CPU and containing a fork bomb, why a container given every capability still could not escape, runc and containerd underneath Docker, the veth pairs and docker0 bridge behind container networking, the idea behind rootless Docker, Podman as a rootless and daemonless alternative to Docker, five Docker security myths — read-only containers and a mounted Docker socket among them — and sandboxing an AI coding agent in Docker. Also covers Podman and rootless Docker. Three entries are private, and it runs newest first. From 2026, and still being added to

videos.name: Streaming Linux Desktops in Docker
videos.description: 6 min · a full Rocky Linux desktop running in a container and opened in the browser, using Kasm’s VNC-based desktop images — setting up the container, using the desktop, then building a custom image on top of it, including getting sudo rights inside. From 2024

videos.name: Podman vs Docker: what’s really different?
videos.description: 6 min · Podman against Docker — a near-identical command line, Podman Desktop and Compose support — then the real differences. Pods group containers (a web server, PHP and MySQL, say) on one network so they start and stop together, and export to Kubernetes YAML. And Podman has no daemon: each container is forked from the podman command and runs rootless by default, where Docker’s daemon runs as root behind a socket, so compromising it hands over the host. Docker keeps the bigger ecosystem, Docker Hub’s images and Swarm, which Podman doesn’t support, and the two can run side by side. From 2024

videos.name: Docker vs Containerd: Understanding the Differences and Choosing the Right Containerization Tool

videos.name: Docker vs LXC
videos.description: 3 min · two ways to use the same namespaces and cgroups — LXC runs a whole persistent distribution like a lightweight VM you can SSH into and manage with systemd, while Docker packages one application into a reproducible image built from a Dockerfile; and you can run Docker inside LXC. From 2026

videos.name: What are a reverse proxy, an API gateway and an ingress controller?
videos.description: 10 min · three names for things that sit in front of your servers, told apart. A reverse proxy forwards each request to the right server by domain or path, and is worth having even with one server for rate limiting, IP filtering, authentication and caching. An ingress controller is a reverse proxy for Kubernetes, with Ingress objects as the routing rules it follows. An API gateway is a reverse proxy in front of microservices that adds service discovery, circuit breaking and combining several backend calls into one response. All three keep your backend services off the open internet. From 2024

videos.name: Caddy in Docker, feature by feature

Rate limiting, caching, layer 4 and GeoIP2 come from plugins rather than stock Caddy. The last video is all the episodes joined into one 4-hour course; the episodes alone come to about 4h 40m. One video is unavailable, and two episodes are both numbered 21. From 2024–2026

videos.name: nginx in Docker, feature by feature

videos.name: MariaDB Administration Tutorial

videos.name: The Complete Bash Scripting Course

Later chapters cover cut, tr, sed, awk and find, set -u and set -x, $PIPESTATUS, sourcing libraries, exit codes against output, parameter expansion, globbing and extglob, brace expansion, printf, regular expressions without grep, mapfile, trap, named pipes, ANSI colours and cursor control, the PS1 prompt and .bashrc, why not to parse ls, and a fork bomb to finish.
